Analysis of cellular immune responses against persistent virus infections.
data.description: The overall aim of these studies is to understand the relationship between immune responses and disease in persistent infection. Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) infection forms the initial focus of this work. The clinical outcomes vary widely, and it is thought that cellular immune responses play a crucial role at various stages of disease. We have recently observed dynamic swings in number and function of CD8 T cells during early disease, and intend to use a combination of tetramer and more classical functional immunological assays to determine how CD8 and CD4 T cells behave at different stages of infection, and after treatment. The studies will focus on small numbers of individuals studied intensively to identify which features (breadth, intensity, secretory or lytic function, distribution, surface phenotype) may influence disease. In parallel it will be possible to observe whether viral variation plays a role in early or established disease, and to what extent over stimulation or exposure to antigen in the liver leading to "exhaustion" or "stunning", is important. It will be important to establish other models of viral infection to assess the generality of each conclusion, and I intend to pursue initial studies made in parvovirus, which have already revealed large populations of CTL during the "memory" phase. This model has the advantage that the virus has a small and highly conserved genome, allowing detailed analysis of breadth and function. Finally, I am to explore novel methods of viral quantitation to complement our studies of quantitation of the immune response, based on direct detection of whole viruses or new methods of nucleic acid detection.

data.title: The molecular manipulation of T lymphocyte activation and function.
data.Sponsor(s): Prof Paul Morgan, Prof Rodney Phillips
data.description: The current major challenge in the study of T cell activation is to understand how the structural and kinetic properties of extracellular recognition events lead to diverse biological consequences. A full understanding of how immune recognition determines T cell function will allow therapeutic intervention to enhance specific immunity or suppress autoreactivity. My work focuses on recognition of natural antigens by human cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTL). Soluble and cell surface expressed wild type and mutant peptide-major histocompatibility complex (MHC) will be used to dissect early intracellular signalling pathways in CTL. I have demonstrated that even subtle differences in the kinetics of extracellular peptide-MHC recognition can cause dramatic differences in the early signalling cascade in CTL leading to outcomes as varied as activation, antagonism, anergy or apoptosis. I will delineate the molecular sequence governing this divergence. Observations in vitro will be examined in vivo. Preliminary experiments in mice demonstrate that the inhibition I observe in vitro with soluble cell surface proteins and altered antigens is applicable in vivo. Further observations suggest that soluble peptide-MHC class I antigenic constructs could be used to target specific autoreactive T cells in vivo. Very little is understood about MHC class I alloreactivity. I have access to well characterised examples of this phenomena. I will examine both the structure and kinetics of the interaction of these T cell receptors (TCRs) with their peptide-MHC I and their corresponding alloreactive ligands. I will compare the molecular signal which leads to activation with both types of ligand. We are now able to successfully manufacture peptide-MHC class II. In the longer term I plan to extend my studies to include T helper lymphocytes. I will also examine the activation of ?d T cells and plan to determine the nature of the ligand recognised by the ?d TCR. Identification of the antigen recognised by these TCRs will assist in establishing a role for this numerically significant, but as yet neglected, T lymphocyte subset. In summary, my expertise will be combined with enormous strengths in molecular immunology in Oxford to initiate a programme of research examining the basic molecular events leading to normal and aberrant lymphocyte activation. The information gained will be used to develop potential therapeutic interventions.

data.title: Auditory object analysis.
data.description: The work addresses the basis for complex sound processing in humans. The work has two components; study of the normal brain processing of patterns of sound objects in time and space, and investigation into clinical disorders where such processing might be deranged. The study of normal brain processing seeks to identify fundamental mechanisms relevant to the processing of sounds such as speech, environmental sounds and music at a level before they acquire meaning. Clinical measures of such processing have the potential to monitor distributed brain function. The work includes assessment of the clinical use of psychophysical measures that do not require processing at the level of sound meaning, and evoked potential measures that do not require conscious participation. I will test the hypothesis that the analysis of temporal and spatial patterns of discrete sounds depends on distinct mechanisms and substrates to those previously identified for the analysis of single sounds. The work involves psychophysics on normal subjects and patients with lesions, and functional imaging. I will develop batteries of tests of temporal and spatial pattern processing suitable for use on patients with lesions, to demonstrate dissociated deficits that reflect distinct mechanisms of processing. Parallel to the lesion work, I will carry out functional imaging of normal subjects to demonstrate the brain basis for such mechanisms. The pattern processing under investigation is a feature of processing beyond the primary cortices, which are relatively spared in many neurodegenerative disorders such as dementia until the late stages. Auditory pattern analysis will be systemically evaluated in a range of disorders. Psychophysical measures will be carried out on subjects with a range of brain conditions. The approach will be extended further to the evaluation of brain function in subjects unable to carry out psychoacoustic testing, using evoked potentials to monitor brain function during the processing of simple sound pattern. This approach will be used in acute and chronic brain dysfunction (coma, persistent vegetative state and dementia). In both the psychophysical and evoked potential studies, the processing of complex sound by the brain will be used as a "window" on acute and chronic brain dysfunction, and related to the phenomenology and outcome of the conditions involved.

data.title: Visual Neglect following Stroke: From Components to Treatments.
data.Sponsor(s): Prof Alan Thompson, Prof Christopher Kennard
data.description: Spatial neglect is a common disabling disorder, acutely affecting up to 70% of stroke patients admitted to hospital. It is characterised by unawareness of objects or people on the side of space opposite brain damage. In many cases neglect hampers rehabilitation and reduces a patient's ability to regain functional independence; but in others it improves rapidly. Although lesions in either cerebral hemisphere - cortical (parietal or frontal) and subcortical - can lead to the disorder, neglect is most enduring following right hemisphere damage. But it is unclear why some patients recover and others do not. There is emerging consensus that neglect is not a unitary disorder, but a syndrome consisting of many different components. The purpose of this research programme is to identify the functional components underlying the neglect syndrome; investigate whether they are related to damage to particular brain regions; identify factors - functional or anatomical - that are associated with poor recovery from neglect; and use this information to guide effective treatment, aimed at specific components of the neglect syndrome. In particular, we shall attempt to establish whether there are fundamental differences between neglect following damage to the left and right hemisphere. We propose to test the hypothesis that, in addition to spatial components, several non-spatial mechanisms underlie neglect, and that these are associated particularly with right hemisphere damage. A major goal of this programme of research will also be to determine the functional components which distinguish parietal from frontal neglect. We shall test the hypothesis that impaired visual processing capacity is associated with parietal lesions, whereas top- down control of visual selection, spatial working memory and sustained attention are disrupted by front damage. In addition to visual mechanisms, we propose that parietal and frontal neglect may be distinguished on the basis of motor components: the former associated with impairments in programming movements and the latter with difficulties in executing them. Selecting between competing movement plans ("motor extinction") may occur in both types of neglect. Finally, the long-term goal of this project is to offer effective treatment targeted at specific components of the neglect syndrome. We propose to use four different methods, including drug therapy. Two of these are aimed at spatial impairments (visual and motor) while the remaining two target non- spatial components using dopamine agonists and acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.

The role of brain area 10 in human cognition.
data.Sponsor(s): Prof Tim Shallice, Prof Jon Driver
data.description: The frontal lobes are often described as the least understood area of the brain, and probably the most problematic region of the frontal lobes is BA10. However, recent findings suggest that the processes supported by BA10 are used in a wide range of quite different situations, and are therefore fundamental to human cognition. Moreover, this view receives support from the association between disturbances in this region and common psychiatric conditions such as depression and schizophrenia. Yet there is no coherent theory about the functions of this large region: this is clearly a marked gap in our knowledge about the brain. A second lacuna appears in our understanding of the comparability of evidence gathered from different methods in cognitive neuroscience. For relatively basic cognitive processes (e.g. those involved in early visual or language processing), prediction from the results of one method to another is conceptually relatively straightforward. However this is not the case for more central processes, and especially for those thought to be supported by frontal lobe structures. Understanding the limits of the expected cross-method concordance is crucial for the development of a cognitive neuroscience of frontal lobe function. Two of the most obvious candidate methods are group adult lesion studies and functional imaging, since they use the same subject base (adult humans). Surprisingly, there is only one study in this subject area that has investigated directly the comparability of findings from the two methods, and the results were not encouraging. Recent findings by this investigator and others however suggest that for BA10 at least, there may be greater predictive validity across method than might at first be expected. For instance, three recent PET studies of situations involving the maintenance and execution of delayed intentions have implicated BA10 in this function. The behavioural corollary of a deficit in this domain would be failures of task switching and an inability to follow one's planned actions. Remarkably, a human group lesion study has demonstrated exactly these problems in patients whose lesions involved BA10. The proposed research will address these issues by testing seven plausible theories concerning the role of BA10 emerging from previous work of the investigator and others, and using a discriminant validity approach. A key component of the investigation is that identical paradigms will be used across two methods (lesion work and functional imaging, both with humans).

data.title: Redox and antioxidant pathways of the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum- characterisation and validation as potential drug targets.
data.Sponsor(s): Prof Paul Hagan, Prof David Barry, Prof John Coggins
data.description: The protozoan parasite Plasmodium falciparum, the causative agent of malaria, resides (for part of its developmental cycle) in human erythrocytes. These stages of the life cycle are responsible for the pathogenicity in humans caused by the parasite. Current knowledge of the biology and biochemistry of these parasites is inaqequate in many respects, but the development of new molecular techniques has made available additional exciting possibilities for investigation of the parasite's metabolism. This project aims to take advantage of these opportunities to analyse anti-oxidants mechanisms of the parasite and determine the roles they play. Plasmodium-infected erythrocytes are under enhanced oxidative stress, due largely to the parasite-mediated haemoglobin digestion. Both the parasite and host cell survive, although they appear to be more vulnerable to additional oxidative stress than are uninfected erythrocytes. The glutathione and thioredoxin systems which co- exist in P. falciparum appear to be key to the parasite's survival as they are involved in the detoxification of reactive oxygen species. One major aim of this project is to determine the extent to which the parasite depends on the functionality of both systems and how far the systems can compensate for each other. Mutant parasites lacking members of both redox systems will be generated and examined in order to determine their exact biological role in the detoxification of reactive oxygen species. Furthermore, the biological functions of the two systems in addition to the defence against oxidative stress will be studied by isolating cellular components which closely interact with the redox systems and to characterise their role in the parasite. This approach will use complementation in yeast and the implementation of the yeast two hybrid system. Structural and mechanistical analyses of the proteins comprising the thioredoxin redox cycle will also be undertaken. Elucidation of key interactions of the proteins with each other, using recombinantly expressed wild-type and mutant proteins, will provide insights into their interactions in the living cell and aid development of new strategies for the rational development of novel antimalarial drugs.

data.title: Genetic regulation of immune responses to BCG vaccination in infants .
data.description: Genetic Regulation of Immune Responses to BCG Vaccination in Infants T helper lymphocytes can be divided into two distinct subsets of effector cells based on their functional capacities and the profile of cytokines they produce. Immunity to mycobacterial infections including tuberculosis is dependent on T helper I (Th1) type cellular immune responses, characterised mainly by interferon-? production. Murine data indicate that Th cell differentiation is genetically regulated. In humans such data is lacking. BCG (Bacillus Calmette- Guerin), a live attenuated vaccine derived from M. bovis, is the most widely used vaccine in the world and the WHO Expanded Programme of Immunisation recommends BCG is given at birth in countries where TB is endemic. However the immunogenicity of BCG in infants had never been investigated. Furthermore, it is generally believed that neonatal immune responses are biased towards Th2. Characterisation of infant immune responses is required for rational development of vaccines. During my 3-year post-doctoral fellowship at the MRC laboratories in The Gambia, Dr Arnaud Marchant and I initiated a series of original studies aimed at characterising the immune response to BCG in newborns. We have shown that, contrary to current opinion, human newborns are able to develop Th1 responses to BCG of a similar magnitude to infants vaccinated later in life and a memory response is induced. Neonatal BCG vaccination is therefore a useful model in which to study the genetic regulation of Th1 immune responses in humans. The material and data I have collected over the last three years provide a unique opportunity to investigate the genetic regulation of human T helper cell responses. This includes a cohort of twins in whom we have shown high heritability for IFN-? production in response to mycobacterial antigens following vaccination at birth, and a cohort of singleton infants in whom IFN-? production also appears to be genetically regulated. The aims of the work described in this proposal are to evaluate the role of host genetic factors in the regulation of human T helper cell immune responses, using neonatal BCG immunisation as a model, and to identify genes involved in this process. I will use two complementary approaches: a) dizygous twin pairs will be used as 'affected sibling pairs' and a genome scan performed to identify chromosomal regions linked to immune responses to BCG, and b) allelic associations between immune responses to BCG and polymorphism in candidate immune response genes will be studied in the cohort of singleton infants given BCG at birth. Allelic association studies will also be used to fine map regions identified in the twin genome scan. Understanding of mechanisms controlling T helper cell differentiation is likely to lead in the long term to therapeutically useful intervention in these processes.

data.title: The molecular mechanism and regulation of transport vesicle formation.
data.description: In eukaryotic cells, the transfer of macromolecules on the secretory and endocytic pathways occurs by the trafficking of membrane bound vesicles between donor and acceptor compartments. The proposed work aims to further the understanding at a molecular level of how vesicles are formed, how this formation is regulated and how cargo molecules are selected for transport. It will utilise an integrated structure/function approach, combining structural (primarily X-ray crystallography but also electron microscopy and NMR), biochemical, biophysical and cell-biological techniques. The most widely studied of these vesicles are clathrin coated vesicles. In these, the membrane is surrounded by a coat consisting of a polyhedral clathrin lattice which is linked to cargo proteins embedded in the membrane by heterotetrameric AP complexes. Four homologous AP complexes have been identified in higher eukaryotes, each of which is associated with trafficking between different organelles. The endocytic AP2 complex consists of two large subunits a and ß2, which can both be subdivided into a trunk domain separated from a 30kDa appendage domain by a short linker, a 50kDa (µ2) subunit and a 17kDa (s2) subunit. They interact with cargo proteins containing Yxx? motifs via µ2, with clathrin via the ßadaptin linker and also recruit accessory proteins that are required for vesicle formation via a appendage domain. In the past two years I have solved the structure of a and ß2 appendage domains and µ2 subunit and elucidated how they interact with their binding partners. The aim of this work is to solve the structure of the remaining subunits of the AP2 complex and subunits and domains of the other AP complexes. These will be used alongside electron microscopy studies on intact complexes and in conjunction with biological/biophysical studies to understand how, in each case, the whole complex carries out its central role in CCV formation. The accessory proteins of CCV formation are also large, multidomain and organelle specific and these will also be targets for studying with an integrated structure/function approach. The COPI vesicle coat system is involved mainly in retrograde transport from the Golgi to the endoplasmic reticulum and displays similarities in function and potentially structure to the AP/clathrin system. Investigating components of the COPI system forms the final part of this project.

data.title: The spindle checkpoint: regulation of mitotic progression and chromosome segregation.
data.description: It is crucial that daughter cells receive a full complement of chromosomes at each cell division. Defects in chromosome segregation lead to aneuploidy and birth defects such as Down's syndrome, and could play a significant role in cancer progression. Spindle microtubule capture by kinetochores of chromosomes is essentially a random process and there are many occasions when more time is required for this to be completed. The spindle checkpoint is a cell cycle control which delays the metaphase to anaphase transition in cells with defects in the interaction between kinetochores and spindle microtubules, thereby providing time for their correction. Molecular components of the spindle checkpoint, the Mad (mitotic arrest defective) and Bub (budding uninhibited by benomyl) proteins, were originally identified through budding yeast genetics. We aim to determine the specific functions of the Mad and Bub proteins, in error detection, signalling and effecting a cell cycle delay. We have identified a number of distinct checkpoint complexes in budding yeast, some of which are present constitutively (Mad1p-Mad2p) and others which are formed at specific cell cycle stages (Cdc20p-Mad2p-Mad3p) or only upon checkpoint activation (Mad1p-Bub1p-Bub3p). We believe that certain complexes have signalling functions and that others inhibit the activity of the anaphase promoting complex (APC). We will use budding yeast to test our models with a combination of molecular genetics and biochemical purification of checkpoint complexes, facilitating study of their regulation and the identification of novel components. Our long term goal is to perform a complete in vitro reconstitution of the checkpoint pathway in budding yeast. In a complementary approach we will use Xenopus egg extracts to determine the relationship of the Mad and Bub proteins and the MAP kinase cascade which clearly forms part of the vertebrate spindle checkpoint. Our work will provide a functional description of this cell cycle control at the molecular level, and models on which studies of the human Mad/Bub homologues can be based.
